blocks.x: The living world is boundlessly vast, fascinating and complex, and even today it is full of mysteries. To make it easier to find one's way through its expanses, scientists have divided this world into a dozen or so kingdoms. A fairly understandable, acceptable and still relevant classification of the living world is that of the English scientist Whittaker (Whittaker, 1969), in which three kingdoms are distinguished according to their mode of nutrition: plants (300 thousand species), fungi (about 1.3 million) and animals (about 1.5–1.7 million).

The world of fungi is one of the largest and least known. Today about 100–300 thousand species have been described, and it is believed that only one in every 5 species has been described. That means there are far more of them.

Unlike plants, nature did not give fungi the miraculous synthesising pigment chlorophyll, thereby limiting their ability to produce organic substances from carbon dioxide and water by harnessing the enormous resources of solar energy. As a result, like other heterotrophic organisms, they were forced to make use of already existing organic matter through direct assimilation. In the course of evolution, fungi have taken excellent advantage of this offer from nature.

Fungi can be found throughout the whole of the earth, wherever there is organic matter. Their wide ecological amplitude is determined by a combination of morphological, physiological and adaptive traits formed over a long evolution. Besides the places with the most suitable living conditions for fungi to thrive (forests, parks, gardens, soil), they are found in the most unexpected places – in the permafrost zone, deep dark underground spaces, caves and grottoes, in mountains above the clouds, in arid deserts and in the depths of the oceans.

In fact, fungi are not so immobile or feeble; at times they are even quite menacing and frightening. Farmers, gardeners, flower growers and foresters are almost constantly confronted with diseases caused by parasitic fungi that inflict a host of losses.

When Fusarium diseases cut down the life of winter crops in the root-collar zone, the damage only becomes visible in spring, when strips of yellowed patches appear in fields of green shoots. Even if a grain does grow, however meagre, it is fit neither for food nor for fodder. The leaves and fruits of cabbages, potatoes, tomatoes and other vegetables are devastated by anthracnose. No less fierce, only harder to notice, are the Verticillium wilts, which choke plants by wilting them. And then there are the "nice" scabs, rusts, smuts and especially powdery mildews – how much damage they do, or how completely they destroy fruit, cereals, vegetables or the seedlings of a future forest. It is hard even to calculate. A great many people and animals suffer from them (especially in warm countries).

What is more, there are many accounts of parasitic fungi that, having got into libraries, museums and archive repositories, mercilessly destroy valuable works of art, books and documents that have survived for centuries or longer while satisfying their vital needs, and damage the most valuable equipment. They wreck houses, break down bridges and help sink ships. These fungi were spoken of with particular ill will by sailors of old, whose wooden ships they often sank. Of course, if a person is prudent and resourceful, the door is closed to dangerous fungi and the losses they cause are small.

On the other hand, many fungi produce valuable medicinal and nutritional substances: antibiotics, vitamins, growth stimulants, enzymes, organic acids, proteins, phosphorus, potassium, etc. Physicians and pharmacologists have long been interested in this; for example, penicillin alone, which has saved millions of lives, exalted fungi as if atoning for the harm done by its kin, drawing special attention to them. About 1000 fungal compounds with antibacterial and antiviral properties or biological activity are currently known, and their medicinal properties are being intensively studied.

Biologists (foresters, farmers, gardeners) have taken an interest in beneficial fungi that destroy insects – and even fungi – harmful to field, orchard, vegetable-garden and forest crops. They successfully make use of their services. It would be hard to imagine the life of bread and pastry bakers, all cooks, brewers and winemakers without yeasts. And what wonderful work fungi do in the soil, loosening it and enriching it with humus.

And the forest (which has sheltered man since time immemorial, clothed him, fed him and protected him from misfortune) is a complex living organism in which harmony and order between plants, animals and especially fungi have been established over millions of years. The forest and fungi are like inseparable twins that cannot live without each other. Every year from 2 to 10 tonnes or more of needles, leaves, twigs, branches and fallen trees fall onto each hectare of forest litter. Here fungi, as the initiators of lignin decomposition, occupy an exceptional place – they are nature's true sanitation workers. Aided by the sun, rain and bacteria, protozoa, insects and other small animals, within a few years or even sooner they turn not only fallen debris but also windthrown trees, stumps and even fine construction timber left unattended into loose forest soil. Some literature sources claim that as many as 80 percent of plant species could not grow well without symbiosis with fungi, or would even languish.
For example, orchids would not even be able to put out a seedling without a fungus, and perhaps even today people would never have seen the flowers of these wonderful plants.
And ceps, orange birch boletes, saffron milkcaps, chanterelles and many other edible and poisonous fungi grow only in the shelter of oak or birch, pine or spruce and certain other trees.

So fungi, one might say, are part of the very organism of the forest and remain important both to the forest and to man. And in the overall cycling of matter in nature they take an active part not only in the decomposition of organic matter, but also in its renewal.

Paleomycologists claim that the first, simplest fungi appeared on earth at the dawn of living organisms (in the Archaean era), approximately 800 million years ago, and mycorrhizal fungi 265 million years ago.

The world of fungi is large and diverse. Fungi vary greatly in size – from those invisible to the naked eye to those weighing a dozen or even several dozen kilograms – and in way of life. Their diversity and distribution are particularly poorly studied. However, macromycetes, and especially cap mushrooms, perhaps because they are larger and more visible, are the best studied of the fungi. In Lithuania about 2500 species of macromycetes have been recorded.

The complex of environmental conditions that determines the way of life, range of distribution and population abundance of a given fungal species is called the species' biotope. The biotopes of individual species differ in size. The smaller the biotope, the smaller the species' chance of spreading, and this determines the survival of that species or even of an individual of it. For this reason every species, as if taught by nature, strives by every means available to it to preserve its innate properties, to improve them, seeking somehow to widen the boundaries of its biotope, but never to narrow them.

The spread of fungi and their adaptation to a given biotope are determined by the following rather important factors: the hyphal structure of the fungal thallus, its growth form, the contact of the thallus with the substrate, the active metabolism of its cells, rapid conquest of the substrate, great adaptive capacity and the ability to produce toxic substances in order to preserve or extend its habitat.

To better understand the relationships between individual fungal species, the fungi themselves, their way of life, their impact on the environment and the possibilities for their use, one must first study fungal species, determine how many there are, and only then classify them, i.e. build a system of the fungal kingdom.

To designate the names of fungi, as with plants, animals and other living organisms, scientific as well as popular literature uses the binary (double) nomenclature introduced by C. Linnaeus in 1733. Every fungus (plant and animal) is named in Latin with two words. For example, in Boletus aereus – the bronze bolete – the first word is the name of the genus, always written with a capital letter, and the second is the species name, written with a lowercase letter.

The natural system of fungi (as of the entire living world) exists only in nature, while scientists, on the basis of the available data and well-founded knowledge, merely try to create as perfect and convincing an artificial classification as possible. At present more than one system of fungal classification has been published; mycologists understand them differently and interpret them in different ways. There is as yet no single system of fungi acceptable to all mycologists.

According to the latest classification, published in 1995, the world of fungi was divided into 11 divisions. However, barely five years later, as new scientific facts accumulated, this system of fungi was refined and corrected. The classification of fungi given by Moreau, 1978 remains popular in the mycological literature even today. Mitosporic fungi lack a sexual stage or have lost it (mostly ascomycetes or some basidiomycetes), and therefore do not form a separate division. In older literature they were placed in a separate division (Deuteromycota). Recently the slime moulds (Myxomycota) have been transferred to the kingdom Protista, and the oomycetes (Oomycota) to the kingdom Stramenopila.

The founder of the systematics of the fungal kingdom is considered to be the Swedish botanist Elias Fries (E. Fries, 1794–1878). In 1821–1822, in his work "Systema mycologicum", he presented a system of fungi whose foundations have not become outdated even now.

The fungal thallus – the mycelium – grows from a spore and is made up of very fine threads, invisible to the naked eye, usually branched, intertwined and tangled, round, pigmented or pale, without cross-walls (septa) in the lower fungi and septate in the higher fungi, called hyphae.

Each segment contains from one to a dozen or so nuclei and cytoplasm with ribosomes, mitochondria and other organelles. Most often the mycelium that grows from a spore consists of two functionally different parts: the substrate (vegetative) part, which supplies the fungus with water and nutrients, and the surface (generative) part – the fruiting body, whose biological purpose is to mature and disperse spores.
In some fungi (for example, some puffballs, truffles and endophytes) both stages of mycelial development take place only within the substrate (soil, wood).

From a biological and physiological point of view, both phases of mycelial development are inseparable parts, very important in the life of the fungus. The vegetative mycelium is usually perennial, while the generative one is annual; only in some, for example many polypores, is it perennial.

In the course of evolutionary processes in nature, the mycelium did not appear all at once; it formed very gradually. The mycelium of the first fungi was very primitive – just a naked protoplast (protoplasm and nucleus), without even a membrane. Even today, after many millions of years, parasitic fungi of such structure are still found in the bodies of animals or plants.

Some fungi, for example yeasts, do not form a vegetative mycelium; it is much more convenient for them to live and reproduce as single, budding segments (cells). However, the original unicellular fungal organisms were puny, delicate little creatures. Over time their physiological and biological needs changed and improved, their morphological traits changed, and the fungi changed too, adapting better and better to environmental conditions. For example, looking at a cep or some other cap mushroom or polypore, it is hard even to imagine what a long evolutionary path it has had to travel.

The vegetative mycelium is a sensitive yet vigorous network of very fine hyphae (1–20 µm and thicker). It is estimated that the length of hyphae in 1 cm3 of soil reaches from 40 to 120 m. That the mycelium of some fungal species is annual and that of others perennial is known even to the more observant mushroom picker who year after year hurries to his favourite spots to gather ceps. The mycelium grows at its tips, spreading radially in all directions; the growth rate of individual species varies, for example in cap mushrooms it is 10–20 cm, rarely 30–50 cm per year.

In the forest people see only the fruiting body of the fungus, i.e. its reproductive organ (the generative mycelium), while its other part – the vegetative mycelium – is settled in the substrate (litter, soil, wood). Incidentally, some fungi are homothallic, when a mycelium grows from a single spore and later also produces fruiting bodies, for example dung fungi.

However, most fungi are heterothallic, i.e. fungi that produce fruiting bodies only during the secondary (dikaryotic) mycelium stage, when the mycelium grows from two spores of different potential (male and female), for example ceps, chanterelles, etc. The secondary mycelium is perennial, whereas in heterothallic fungi a mycelium grown from a single spore is short-lived and does not form or produce fruiting body primordia.

The nature and biological purpose of the fruiting body is to form, mature and disperse spores. Thus it is nature's foster child, raised and perfected by nature, and as if in return for this it must mature and disperse as many spores as possible, since this is extraordinarily important in the life of every fungal species. The shape, size and colour of the fruiting bodies of individual species vary greatly, depending on environmental conditions and way of life. Even as a primordium, the fruiting body already has two missions – to mature spores and to disperse them.

The lifespan of a fruiting body, except for some polypores, is very short (from a few hours to a dozen or so days), and people are convinced that mushrooms grow very fast. This is partly true. But what they call a mushroom is only the above-ground part of the fungus – the fruiting body, which under good conditions does indeed grow quickly.
But how does the vegetative mycelium, which is invisible to us, live? How it has overwintered and when it gets around to growing can only be guessed.

It is believed that it wakes up in early spring and starts growing together with all living nature when the soil temperature rises to 5–8 °C, while its intensive life begins at no less than 15–18 °C. Only after a few months do the fruiting body primordia begin to form; being of different ages and at different depths, they begin to form fruiting bodies, which emerge at the surface at different times. Only from this moment, given sufficient warmth and moisture, does a cep or an orange birch bolete or another cap mushroom really grow very quickly, its cap increasing by 1.5 to 5 cm per day. For the vegetative mycelium to recover, grow stronger and gain new potential vital forces, the appropriate amount of warmth, moisture and light is needed; a considerable role is also played by CO2 and the exchange of other gases, even windiness and the whole microclimate.

So a cep, a birch bolete, a chanterelle, a Russula or any other mushroom, like a cucumber, a cabbage or a potato, does not grow in a few days but over several months. When picking mushrooms, let us know this and be more careful: let us not tear up the litter, rummage in the moss or destroy fungal habitats while searching for tiny ceps or chanterelles.
The world of fungi is very diverse; many of them differ not only in their structure but also in the peculiarities of their life.
According to their mode of nutrition, fungi are divided into saprotrophic, parasitic (biotrophic) and mycorrhizal (mycosymbiotrophic).

Fallen leaves, needles, branches, snags and windthrown trees in forests, parks and even gardens and fields, or valuable timber from trees that grew for decades, sometimes even centuries, left too long unattended, dead herbaceous cover, excrement and small animal organisms – all this is food for saprotrophs.

Saprotrophs, as active sanitation workers of the environment, play an enormous role in nature. It has been calculated that every year from 50 to 100 billion tonnes of organic matter is synthesised in various ecosystems (forests, fields, waters, etc.), most of it of plant origin. In its decomposition, especially of lignin and cellulose, the main role belongs to fungi. In the biogeocoenosis, fungi are decomposers and users of organic and inorganic compounds, and they are food for plants, bacteria, invertebrates and small vertebrates. Saprotrophs are the most widespread group of fungi in nature. They were the first fungi on earth. Many of them are edible.

Parasitic fungi feed on the juices of living organisms (plants, animals). They live in the bodies of plants, animals and even humans. These include rusts, scabs, smuts, powdery mildews, downy mildews, etc. These fungi cause particularly great damage and losses to agriculture. Not infrequently, parasites cover the fertile part of the fruiting body of ceps, Russula and other mushrooms – the hymenophore – with a yellowish, greenish, white or greyish layer (mould). In killing their victim, they not only take its life, but also its chance to disperse spores and leave offspring.

These are cannibal fungi that destroy their own kin. Or perhaps this is nature's design – the self-regulation of fungi. Edible mushrooms attacked by a parasite lose their nutritional value, become unfit for consumption and sometimes become poisonous. Even the nimble house fly cannot escape the snares of these fungi, which envelop its body as if with down and glue it to the window pane. This most often happens in autumn. A similar fate befalls many insect species living in the forest, meadow or farmstead.

Never mind catching a fly or some other insect – even mighty trees, even century-old oaks, cannot withstand an attack by a parasitic fungus. A scratch on the root collar, trunk or a branch, or some other injury, is for the honey fungus an open gateway to the heart of the oak. Who would think that the honey fungus rhizomorphs – cords capable of jumping from one tree to another – hidden under the forest litter, penetrate between the bark and the wood and, slowly but relentlessly, fell the tree more terribly than a woodcutter. Not one or two, but clusters, troops, hundreds of fruiting bodies adorned with yellowish caps arouse no distrust or suspicion; on the contrary, with their edible qualities they awaken sympathy, which is why the fungus is even affectionately called "kelmutis" ("little stump one"), almost "gerutis" ("good little one").

As the years pass, although the oak will put up a fierce resistance, one day it will be defeated and, helped by a gust of wind, will crash to the ground. On it, replacing one another, ever more fungi will settle, and the "benefactor" honey fungus, becoming a saprotroph, will not leave either but will further multiply its troops, until finally, having sucked out everything useful, they will pass the crumbs on to the grass, which, growing lush, will seem to hurry to hide all traces of the tragedy.

Mycorrhizal fungi, unlike saprotrophs or parasites, are quite different: they live in friendly coexistence with plants, especially trees and shrubs, form mycorrhiza (a symbiosis of fungus and plant) and not only do not harm each other, but even help each other and are mutually beneficial.

Using the radioactive isotope method, it has been established that fungi obtain from trees carbohydrates – organic nutrients they need very much – and in exchange, as it were, help the tree to supply itself more easily with water and mineral substances (N, P, Ca, K, Na). Of course, as in all cases of exchange, signs of parasitism have been observed not only on the part of the fungus, but also on the part of the tree. However, this does not overshadow the essence of this mutually beneficial phenomenon.

At present more than 2000 plant species have been recorded that seek close association with fungi, and a considerable proportion maintain even very close and beneficial relationships. Some sources indicate that as many as 80 percent of plants tend to form mycorrhiza.

Mycorrhiza can be of several types: endomycorrhiza (internal), when the mycelium settles in the fine rootlets or root hairs between the cells without changing either the internal or the external morphological features of the rootlet or root hair; and ectomycorrhiza (external), when the mycelium wraps around them from the outside (as if the rootlet or root hair were wearing a frayed glove or a felted sock) but without penetrating inside them, thereby increasing the absorbing surface of the root hairs and fine rootlets of almost all the coniferous and broadleaved trees and some shrubs growing in Lithuania by more than several or even 10 times. Of course, because of the hyphal sheath that forms, the morphological features of the fine rootlets and root hairs change somewhat. Depending on the fungal species, the hyphal sheath formed around the rootlet or root hair has its own distinctive structure, surface pattern (texture) and colour. It is believed that 5–6 thousand fungal species form ectomycorrhiza, and it is of particularly great importance to trees and to all natural forest ecosystems in the temperate zone.

Micromycetes are the allies of herbaceous plants (mostly through endomycorrhiza), while macromycetes are the allies of woody plants. This is a very interesting phenomenon in the life of fungi and plants. English scientists noticed that when the leaves of a birch were stripped, mushrooms stopped growing under it, but when the birch leafed out again, carbohydrate production in the tree resumed and the mushrooms began to grow again.

Later still they established that fungi need not only carbohydrates obtained through the roots, but also other growth-promoting substances. It has also been observed that tree roots, while absorbing nutrients, release their own phytopathogenic "agents" into the rhizosphere that are harmful to soil microorganisms and sometimes even to another tree growing nearby. Or perhaps this is how mycorrhizal fungi serve their host – by destroying unwanted organisms. It has been established that mycorrhizal fungi do not leave their benefactor host from early spring to late autumn, even for many years in a row. Depending on the age of the tree and the composition of the soil, the fungal species gradually change too. Which of them – the tree or the fungus – is more faithful and more useful to the other is for now known only to themselves.

An observant mushroom picker knows that some mushrooms grow only under certain trees, others only under other trees, or that the same mushrooms grow in both coniferous and broadleaved forests. It has also been observed that at the base of the stem of a mycorrhizal mushroom (for example, a cep) there are fewer loose mycelial hyphae than in a saprotrophic one – some kind of Clitocybe, which is sometimes not even easy to pull out.

Mycorrhizal fungi are very faithful to their host plant. When it dies, the fungus withdraws too, most often giving way to saprotrophs. There are more forms of mycorrhiza. This phenomenon has recently been studied intensively; elucidating it as fully as possible is very important from both a theoretical and a practical point of view, especially for foresters planting new forest areas. It is gratifying that ectomycorrhiza is also being studied in Lithuania – at the Institute of Botany.

It has been noticed that the mode of nutrition of many fungi is not strictly defined. For example, the variegated Tricholoma, when growing in a broadleaved forest, lives as a saprotroph, and in a coniferous one as a mycorrhizal fungus. The oyster mushroom and the velvet shank cover stumps, branches and rotting trunks in clusters, but given the chance, like the common honey fungus, they readily attack living trees, for example the soft, juicy wood of limes and alders. Or the "good little" common honey fungus in forests, where there is a wider choice, more often makes use of its saprotrophic properties, whereas in parks, and especially in gardens, on the contrary, it more often reveals its true parasitic way of life. It is believed that saprotrophic, biotrophic and mycorrhizal fungi inherited this way of life from their ancestors.

Although mushrooms have been eaten since time immemorial – they are mentioned in ancient writings 4–5 hundred years before our era – even today opinions about their nutritional value differ. Some speak up for the original taste and aroma of mushrooms and compare them with fish and meat dishes, while others regard them with caution – as a low-value food product.

French chefs claim that the aromatic substances of mushrooms and their sauces are without equal: they stimulate the secretion of gastric juices, increase appetite and improve the digestion of other foods. Is that not an advantage? Many cooks, some experts and specialists in the nutritional value of mushrooms, and especially many mushroom gourmets, are probably not mistaken in believing that mushrooms are a valuable food product. This is also confirmed by research in scientific laboratories, including Lithuanian ones.

As with every food product, the value of mushrooms depends not only on their chemical composition, but also on the ratio of beneficial elements (amino acids, especially the essential ones, which the human body obtains only from food, etc.).

This is determined by the mushroom's habitat, climatic conditions and the season. In this respect some mushroom species are not inferior to, or even surpass, the most valuable vegetables, some fruits and other food products.

Mushrooms contain no fewer mineral substances than vegetables or fruits, and in their content of phosphorus, potassium and calcium they are equal to fish. Only fats and carbohydrates are scarce in mushrooms.
Mushrooms contain iron, manganese, cobalt, copper and zinc, which are much needed by the human body, especially in autumn and winter. They contain all the amino acids the human body needs.
It is enough to eat 60 g of dry (dried) mushrooms, not necessarily just ceps, and our body already receives its daily requirement of mineral substances and amino acids.

Mushrooms are rich in protein: proteins make up the main part of the dry matter (about 80 percent), while the aromatic substances, of which there are more than 40 (according to some data, as many as 52), give them a specific, indescribably pleasant aroma unlike that of other foods.

Mushrooms contain many vitamins (B1, B2, PP, C, A, D, U), enzymes and organic acids. Dried ceps contain more protein than bread, groats or beef. Of particular importance is the amino acid lecithin, which prevents harmful cholesterol from accumulating in the human body.
Young mushrooms are more nutritious, and the cap is more valuable than the stem. In many mushrooms the stem is woody, contains a lot of chitin and is not eaten at all.
Mushroom dishes are not recommended for people suffering from chronic diseases of the stomach, liver, intestines or kidneys, nor for elderly, sedentary people or for children.

Mushrooms, like cepelinai, are a tasty, tempting but hard-to-digest food, so one should not eat too much of them. In addition, heavy metals, especially lead, and radionuclides – radium, caesium, strontium – reduce the value of some mushrooms and oblige us to be careful. But the value of mushrooms is reduced most of all by indigestible chitin (fungin), which makes up from 3 to 6 percent of the walls of fungal hyphae. Mushrooms also contain a lot of water – 84–95 percent.

About 400 species of edible mushrooms grow in Lithuania, but only about 100–120 species are worth eating; the others are of little value – their fruiting bodies are very small, they are rarely found or grow in small quantities.

Learning to recognise edible mushrooms is possible only by spending time with experienced mushroom experts, reading books and atlases and visiting mushroom exhibitions. Lithuanian forests are rich in mushrooms, so one should not limit oneself to just a few or a dozen or so species.
In 1948 the Russian mycologist Dr. B. P. Vasilkov divided edible mushrooms into 4 categories according to their nutritional value, taste, distribution and traditions of consumption.

This was a subjective division, since the biochemical composition of many edible mushrooms, which determines their nutritional value, was not yet known, and so some mushroom species ended up in one category or another without justification.
The opinions of many of the world's mycologists on this question did not coincide, so this classification was not widely used either.

The biochemical properties of edible mushrooms are still far from fully studied even today, so in the world people mostly rely on the assessment of edible and poisonous mushrooms used in the German mycological literature, which is based on practical laboratory research, especially since the biochemical properties of poisonous, and particularly dangerous, mushrooms have been studied comparatively thoroughly.

EDIBLE, OF LITTLE VALUE – mushrooms whose fruiting bodies are small and rarely found, and which, when prepared as food, have an unremarkable taste;EDIBLE, VALUABLE – mushrooms with a pleasant taste, eaten fresh, salted, pickled, frozen or otherwise prepared, not uncommon;EDIBLE, VERY VALUABLE – mushrooms with a pleasant aroma and taste, eaten fresh, dried, pickled, frozen, smoked or prepared as food in other ways, not uncommon;INEDIBLE – mushrooms that do not cause poisoning because they contain no poisonous substances, but that can cause unpleasant, painful sensations (fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea);POISONOUS – mushrooms containing mildly poisonous substances that are dangerous to human health or even life, e.g. some Amanitas, Clitocybe funnels, Tricholoma knights and Inocybe fibrecaps;VERY POISONOUS – mushrooms containing highly poisonous substances that are dangerous to human health and life, e.g. the death cap;NUTRITIONAL VALUE UNKNOWN – mushrooms that cannot be classed as poisonous, edible or inedible, and that are sometimes listed in the literature as edible and in other sources as inedible.

The world of mushrooms also contains very poisonous and treacherous species that have entered human history as hostages of mysterious "cutthroats" and have contributed to the crippling of many people's lives or even to their deaths.
More than 1000 species of poisonous mushrooms grow in Europe; in our forests, parks and gardens over 100 are known so far, of which 20–30 are very dangerous to human life.

However, these are only approximate figures, because there is no strict boundary between inedible and poisonous, and moreover the harmful properties of only a few poisonous mushrooms have been studied. There is no need to fear poisonous mushrooms – you just need to know them. They are not a snake or a scorpion, a hornet or even the good little bee, which, when carelessly stepped on, squeezed or otherwise provoked, will defend themselves with a venomous bite.

Very poisonous are the death cap and the destroying angel, the livid pinkgill (Entoloma), the spruce conecap, the blushing (Patouillard's) fibrecap, the fierce and poisonous funnels and some others. Even 2–3 such mushrooms that get into the pot are, without any exception, equally deadly to the young, adults and the old. A single fruiting body of the blushing fibrecap weighing 30–100 g is mortally dangerous to a person weighing 70 kg.

These mushrooms are now well studied, and it is known which of the substances they contain are poisonous; for example, in the most dangerous mushroom – the death cap – as many as 16 poisonous substances have been identified, 7 of them especially dangerous: amanitins, amanin, phalloidin, phallacidin, etc. It is enough to eat a fruiting body weighing 50 g, containing 5–7 mg of amatoxins alone, which do not dissolve in boiling water – and this is already a lethal dose for a human (in a 100 g fruiting body the amount of amatoxins is doubled). The literature states that of 562 cases of poisoning, 282 were fatal. The other mushrooms mentioned have similar properties.

A mushroom's toxicity depends on where it grows and on its age and size: the younger it is, the more terrible. The most terrible thing is that when poisoned by these mushrooms, one feels ill only when it is already too late – after several or even a dozen or more hours, and sometimes even after 2 days or later, when the poison has already been absorbed into the blood and has damaged the functioning of the liver and brain.

In such cases it is almost impossible to save oneself. The poison has already done its dark work. Yet however repulsive the Amanitas and other toadstool-looking poisonous mushrooms may appear, and although many people know them well, these tricksters still sneak into the basket and through their deceit cause a great deal of trouble for the inattentive mushroom picker. Every year in Lithuania there are still several cases of poisoning, and then even doctors are sometimes powerless to save a life.
In the simplest and most understandable way, poisonous mushrooms can be divided into three groups according to the symptoms of poisoning:

a) mushrooms that merely irritate the digestive tract (some bitter milkcaps, brittlegills). After eating them, within 1–2 hours the temperature rises and the patient vomits and has diarrhoea, but recovers after a couple of days;

b) mushrooms whose poisons act on the nervous system (the fly agaric, the false death cap, the blusher). After eating them, within 2–3 hours nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea begin, the pupils dilate and hallucinations appear; if medical help is given quickly, such patients recover without much difficulty;

c) mushrooms whose poisons (amatoxins, phallotoxins, especially phalloidin, amanitin) destroy blood, liver or brain cells (the death cap, the destroying angel, the livid pinkgill, the blushing fibrecap, the spruce conecap). 8–24 or even 48 hours or more after the meal, liver function is disrupted (the liver hardens), and pain, convulsions, vomiting and diarrhoea appear, followed by loss of consciousness; the symptoms subside somewhat and then worsen again, attacks of pain recur and the temperature rises.

It should be borne in mind that soggy, maggot-ridden mushrooms or mushrooms nipped by several frosts, especially those growing in late autumn and later (in December), can also cause severe poisoning – just like spoiled meat, fish or butter. In the realm of the gilled mushrooms, the ones to be most feared are the Amanitas, the pinkgills, the fibrecaps, the funnels and the rollrims.

Among the boletes and the brittlegill family, of which about 130 species grow in Lithuania, there are no especially dangerous ones. Of the mushrooms growing in spring, the most dangerous is the false morel. It has been found to contain the poisonous substance gyromitrin, which does not break down completely when boiled, so sometimes one can be poisoned even by false morels that have been boiled twice. When the mushrooms are dried (in a shady place, but only a non-residential one), the gyromitrin evaporates over 2–3 months and its toxicity is greatly reduced.

In the event of mushroom poisoning, put the patient to bed immediately, because heart function is impaired in all cases; place a hot-water bottle at the feet and on the abdomen, give tea or coffee to strengthen the heart, and categorically avoid alcoholic drinks. Induce vomiting and diarrhoea artificially and see a doctor as quickly as possible.

The tribes of ancient Mexico, India, China and Egypt used hallucination-inducing mushrooms that affected their senses, behaviour, psyche and outlook. These properties of mushrooms were also known to the Vikings of northern Scandinavia, who used them when going into battle to raise their spirits.

The Yakuts, Nenets, Eskimos and Chukchi used these mushrooms when going out hunting, or even in everyday life as an intoxicant instead of alcohol. The Indian tribes of Central America exalted mushrooms so highly that they erected statues and temples to them.
Even today huge mushroom-shaped stone statues stand in Guatemala, beside which, in ancient times, religious rites were performed after eating hallucinogenic mushrooms.

In the Indians' belief, the mushrooms tore them away from the earth and brought them closer to the gods they had created. Even now, in those countries, rites of faith connected with the worship of mushrooms and the hallucinations they induce, which are kept secret, have not only survived in some people's consciousness but are still performed.

Such phenomena also attracted the interest of mycologists and physicians. The French mycologist H. Heim and the Americans R. G. Wasson (a physician) and A. Weil (a physician, neuropathologist and writer) succeeded in identifying the hallucination-inducing mushrooms. They studied the available scientific knowledge about the use of hallucinogenic mushrooms in ritual ceremonies by the Indians of Mexico and South America, ate these mushrooms themselves, took part in their rites, experienced the effects of the mushrooms themselves and described all this in detail in several books.

These are mostly small mushrooms of the genus Psilocybe, which have strong hallucinogenic properties, but their effect manifests itself somewhat differently from that of LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide). In these and in mushrooms of some other genera with such properties, strong hallucinogenic substances have been found: psilocin, psilocybin, ibotenic acid, muscarine, muscarone, muscimol and bufotenine.

In small amounts these substances are widely used in psychotherapy; they activate serotonin activity in the brain and improve a person's condition. For this purpose, to obtain the psychotropic substances mentioned, the Cuban Psilocybe (Psilocybe cubensis), for example, which grows naturally in Cuba, is specially cultivated artificially (in greenhouses) in large quantities.
It is the largest of the Psilocybe species growing in the wild; its cap grows from a few to 10 or even more than a dozen centimetres in diameter.
Such hallucinogenic mushrooms do not grow in Lithuania, but other Psilocybe species growing here, some Amanitas and some other mushrooms have similar, though more weakly expressed, properties.

People noticed long ago that chanterelles and some other mushrooms grow in circles, in rings, and that inside and around them a much greener and lusher strip of grass ripples when stirred by even the slightest breeze.

In the Middle Ages, and especially even earlier, this frightened people, because it was explained as hellish circles trampled out by the inhabitants of hell themselves. Witches were often blamed for this – supposedly it was the work of their nocturnal rituals and pranks. For this reason mushroom circles are called "witches' circles", sometimes "witches' rings".

For a very long time, up to the beginning of the last century, it was believed that only supernatural forces could draw such a precise circular line in forests or fields, where the grass also grows in alternation – now lush and deep green, now withered. People were afraid to approach such rings, and only the bolder ones were glad to cut plenty of chanterelles or other mushrooms there.

Only at the beginning of the last century did it become clear that this is not the work of witches or Satan, but an expression of the normal way of life of the common fairy ring champignon (Marasmius oreades) and many other mushrooms. About 15–20 percent of cap mushrooms form so-called "witches' circles". Once it was learned that each year the mycelium grows radially from a germinated spore in all directions by 10–20 cm, and in some mushrooms even more, the cause of the appearance of "witches' circles" was easily revealed.

Many cap mushrooms grow in rings, but not necessarily in the geometric configuration of a regular circle. Particularly regular circles are formed by the fairy ring champignon, the parasol, some plempė, gijabudė and guotė species, funnels and certain other mushrooms that struck terror in the old days.

Strange as it may seem, even today "witches' circles" frighten some people. For example, in 2002 in the Pakruojis district a similar phenomenon was noticed in a large field of grain, and even astrophysicists and psychics took part in explaining it, but mycologists, who could have helped to reveal the essence of the phenomenon, were not invited. Of course, it is very strange why no mushroom rings had been noticed in these fields in earlier years.

The mycelium of many cap mushrooms is perennial and survives for several decades, and the literature describes "witches' circles" that are 600 years old or older. For example, in the prairies of the state of Colorado (USA) in 1917 a 500-year-old "witches' circle" was identified, whose diameter reached 200 m.
So how do "witches' circles" form, and why does lush green grass grow inside them and surround them on the outside?

This is because the mycelium grows radially, in a ring. The most vigorous part of the mycelium is in the peripheral part of the regular ring, in a 20–30 cm zone; here it is best developed and has accumulated the most nutrients, and here the primordia of the fruiting bodies form, from which only mushrooms grow, while grass is hardly to be seen. The dense mycelial tangle that develops in this zone (20–30 cm) uses up all the moisture, leaving none for the roots of the grasses, and a so-called physiological drought arises in the zone, which prevents grasses from growing. In addition, a high concentration of nitrogen and harmful substances secreted by the mycelium has been found in this zone, poisoning the grass roots, which is why they no longer grow.

The young, vigorous mycelium, using hydrolytic enzymes, breaks down the proteins and other organic substances in the soil beyond this mycelial zone and decomposes them into ammonia, which the bacteria present convert into nitrates easily absorbed by grasses; as a result the grass grows lushly and is a striking, deep green colour.

Inside the ring, when the old mycelium has died off and decomposed, many nitrogenous substances are also released; these are easily absorbed by herbaceous plants, which turn greener and lusher than those growing outside the rings. In this way the mycelium, having extracted during the growing season in its new location (the 20–30 cm zone) everything that was useful, necessary and accessible to it, and having grown a new generation of fruiting bodies, will keep spreading, again supply itself with essential food and again raise its offspring.
Mushrooms growing in rings no longer frighten mushroom pickers, but only delight them.

h: Where, When and How to Pick Mushrooms

blocks.x: Where? In the forest, sometimes in a meadow or pasture – a mycologist or an experienced mushroom picker would say. Some forests have more, others fewer; only the picker's own individual experience is the best adviser. When you go out mushroom picking, do not look for an all-knowing adviser, and do not turn to a psychic or a fortune-teller. It will not help. You will hardly find a kind-hearted adviser. Only experience, intuition, and perhaps sometimes a prophetic dream are the best advisers.

A balanced amount of moisture and warmth is the guarantee of mushroom growth. And when mushrooms are growing, even an inexperienced picker will always find more or fewer of them. The best time of day for mushroom picking is early morning, when the forest is still damp and cool, when glistening drops of water fall from branches or leaves, exposing shiny, slimy mushroom caps. Refreshed by the morning dew, mushrooms are juicier, firmer, and perhaps even easier to spot than in the sunlit litter later in the day. In the morning even the smallest mound of earth covered with leaves will stop you, make you look around, and not infrequently delight you with a handsome cep hiding a few steps away, rising from under the leaves or moss. If damp and warm, but not too hot, weather has set in for a longer time and the nights are not cold, mushrooms grow in old and young, dense and sparse forests alike.

If it is rather dry and cold, even though there is enough moisture, it is better to look for them in the forest thicket and not to worry too much about a small haul. Mushrooms do not like such weather.

If there are mushrooms at the market, it is a sign that it is time to go mushroom picking, to spend time in the forest and enjoy its bounty. The market is a fairly good barometer of the mushroom season. Of course, in May and even in early June one should not rush into the forest, because the mycelium, except in rare years, has not yet grown strong enough to produce many mushrooms. At this time mushroom picking is not advisable (just as fishing during fish spawning or hunting during the birds' nesting period); the vegetative mycelium is growing intensively, preparing for the future harvest, and one should not yet trample the litter or step on a mushroom's "head". Misty, damp weather is the most suitable for mushrooms to grow and for picking them.

How to dress? As lightly and comfortably as possible. A mushroom picker dressed in waterproof clothing, wearing high-topped footwear and definitely wrapped in a headscarf or wearing a hat, will feel more comfortable crawling about and bending under branches, walking among the bushes, searching for the mysterious habitats of mushrooms. Pick only mushrooms you know well, and preferably only into wooden or plastic baskets. Plastic or metal buckets and plastic bags should not be used, because mushrooms contain a lot of water and are also damp on the outside, so after a few hours in such containers they heat up faster, get maggoty, lose their good appearance, a lot of bacteria appear in them and their nutritional value declines.

Should you pull up or cut a mushroom? The mushroom is cut right at the ground or carefully pulled out, but not broken off. If the cap is broken off, bacteria and other microorganisms quickly attack the damaged part of the stem, spoiling not only it but also the vegetative mycelium at its base. Still, it is better to cut the mushroom, and this method is more widespread, because you can see at once whether the mushroom is sound or maggoty. The small part of the stem left in the litter poses no danger to the vegetative mycelium. In addition, cleaner mushrooms go into the basket.

It is advisable for the mushroom picker to walk with the sun behind them on a sunny day, as the mushrooms are then easier to see in the sunlit litter, and to touch the branches of trees and shrubs as little as possible and not to wade through wet grassy places, where mushrooms do not always grow, because spiders, flies, bugs and especially ticks lurk there more often, as well as some other midges waiting for prey or simply hidden insects.

Ticks, which frighten us most and are, moreover, quite dangerous, are most fond of young, grassy aspen groves, clearings and thickets of raspberries and nettles; they are found even in pastures. They usually settle on the leaves and stems of grasses or on shrubs (at a height of 25 cm – 1 m) growing beside little roads and paths where it is easier for a small animal to run through or for a mushroom or berry picker to pass.

It is not advisable to pick mushrooms in forests closer than 300–500 m from major highways and roads, where passing cars emit a lot of lead, chromium, nickel, cobalt and other pollutants, a considerable part of which is absorbed by mushrooms. In forests sprayed with arboricides, mushroom picking, as well as gathering berries or medicinal herbs, is permitted only after 10 months. Where forests have been sprayed with arboricides, a warning sign must always be posted. In the forest, the mushroom picker must be not only careful but also attentive, and must not lose their bearings under the spell of the forest and the mushrooms. That is why it is very useful for a mushroom picker to know a few things:

• pick for food only mushrooms you know well that are not maggoty or old; do not risk your own health or that of your family, good friends or neighbours; • it is dangerous to pick and eat mushrooms frozen by several successive frosts, in which protein breakdown has begun and amines and amides – poisonous substances – have formed; • you must not press a dubious opinion about one mushroom or another on another mushroom picker; • mushroom picking is not permitted in strict nature reserves, or in the strictly protected areas of national parks and other protected sites; • do not pick mushrooms that are protected – listed in the Red Data Book of Lithuania; • do not pull up a cep whose cap is less than 1.5 cm in diameter, or a chanterelle under 1 cm;• you must not destroy the forest litter, which is home not only to mushrooms but also to other small forest animals;• it is not advisable to pick mushrooms along roadsides, highway verges or near railways, because the mushrooms growing there have accumulated far more pollutants than those growing in a forest 200–500 m away or farther; • it has been established that mushrooms accumulate 4–5 times or more radioactive caesium than plants. The source of lead, cadmium, nickel, chromium and caesium is the forest litter, while arsenic, manganese and iron accumulate deeper in the substrate, but all of them are accessible to mushrooms; • more susceptible to pollutants are the gypsy mushroom, the bay bolete, the lelijinė stirnabudė, the common honey fungus and the birch knight. In parboiled mushrooms the pollutants are reduced by half, if the water is poured off; • after pulling up a mushroom, you must clean the earthy part of the stem thoroughly so that it does not dirty the other mushrooms you have gathered; moreover, humus-rich soil may contain the bacteria that cause botulism (Clostridium botulinum); • do not believe the advice that mushrooms growing on stumps, snags or windthrown trees are supposedly poisonous – this is not true: the honey fungi (the common honey fungus, the sheathed woodtuft, the velvet shank), the oyster mushroom and some scalycaps are tasty mushrooms; • do not believe the claim that all young mushrooms are edible, because the death cap, the blushing (Patouillard's) fibrecap, the livid pinkgill and other poisonous mushrooms are many times more poisonous when young than when old; • sometimes the press, radio or television, seeking popularity, present dubious or even completely false impressions of one mushroom picker or another; for example, the radio reports that edible truffles have been found somewhere in the Šakiai district (or perhaps they were some hart's truffles, false truffles or even poisonous earthballs), or that 3000 ceps were found on a plot of one are (perhaps they were some slippery jacks). Conditions in Lithuania seem too harsh for the truffle to grow, and finding so many ceps on a small plot is unbelievable. Such information should not be given to the public without consulting mycologists; • when preparing to go mushroom picking, especially in unfamiliar forests, do not forget a compass, which will help a great deal if you get lost. On arriving in the forest, always memorise the name of the nearest settlement or forest; • a forest compartment post, especially one standing at the intersection of compartments, is the best sign for someone who is lost to get their bearings: the smallest number is on the north side. Standing facing this number, you will know that on your right is west, on your left is east, and behind you is north; • while picking mushrooms it is advisable to check the exposed parts of your body every 2 hours, and after returning from the forest – your whole body; in addition, quickly change into other clothes in a non-residential room, and shake out the clothes you have taken off and dry them in the corridor or hallway, hung away from other clothes or footwear being worn; • if a tick has attached itself, do not smear it with either kerosene or grease – this will only make it harder to pull out. After removing it, the bite site is dabbed with alcohol, eau de cologne or iodine; if you suspect the tick may be infected, put it in a small bottle and see a doctor.

h: A Few Tips for the Cook

blocks.x: Mushrooms contain a lot of water, proteins, mineral substances and organic acids, so picked mushrooms are easily attacked by moulds, by the larvae inside them and even by bacteria.

On returning from the forest, you must deal with the mushrooms as quickly as possible, putting all other work aside. They must not be left until the next day, and if there is no other way out or you have not managed to deal with them in time, they must be taken out of the baskets for the night and spread out loosely in a cold, dark cellar or another cool room.
Mushrooms can be dried, salted, pickled or frozen. They are made into juices, chopped mushroom preparations, flour and other semi-finished products.

There is plenty of literature on how to use mushrooms and prepare them for a meal or as supplies for the winter, and many tips in magazines, newspapers and cookery guides. Incidentally, cooks themselves are also well informed, each more inventive than the next; they have their own tried and tested methods and gladly share their experience with others. A few useful tips:

• process fresh mushrooms that have been gathered or bought for food as quickly as possible; • do not wash ceps, orange birch boletes, birch boletes or slippery jacks too much: over time water soaks into them, the mushrooms become watery and soft and lose some of their aroma; • slippery jacks, brittlegills and other mushrooms whose skin peels easily should be peeled, since this removes a considerable part of the bitter and other substances unnecessary for food; • ceps, slippery jacks, orange birch boletes, parasol mushrooms and non-bitter brittlegills can be fried without parboiling or after merely pouring boiling water over them; • clean mushrooms with a stainless steel knife; • soak bitter-tasting brittlegills and milkcaps for several (or a dozen or so) hours, changing the water 1–3 times, then parboil them and pour off the water they were boiled in; • boil and fry them over a low heat in closed enamelled pans for no longer than 20–30 min.; when fried longer, mushrooms become tough, harder to digest and less well absorbed, and their nutritional value declines; • citric acid lightens colour, so it should be used when parboiling orange birch boletes, yellow slippery jacks (makavykai), tamprieji baravykai (firm boletes), yellowfoots, some knights and other mushrooms that darken; • butter, onions and a little garlic improve the aromatic and flavour qualities of mushrooms; • eat prepared mushroom dishes on the same day: in the refrigerator mushroom dishes lose their aromatic qualities, so it is better to keep mushrooms raw and fresh, without parboiling; • all mushrooms are tastier and better absorbed by the body when chopped as finely as possible; • dried mushrooms will not lose their value for several years if you keep them in an airtight, dark container, especially a glass one; • salted and pickled mushrooms should be eaten within a year; • do not buy or sell pickled and salted mushrooms at markets, because poisonous ones may also be acquired there – buy mushrooms only in shops; • mushrooms are frozen at a temperature no higher than -18 °C; only young, firm, non-watery mushrooms are frozen (ceps, slippery jacks, orange birch boletes, chanterelles and some others), cleaned thoroughly and wrapped in a sheet of foil; • fry (stew) mushrooms only in butter, by no means in vegetable oil; frozen mushrooms can be kept for no longer than 3–4 months; • mushrooms are dried at a high (60–70 °C) temperature in a ventilated room; • eating dishes of pickled, salted or otherwise preserved, and even freshly prepared, mushrooms that have been washed uncleanly and not cooked well enough can cause botulism; illness sets in after the meal, most often after 10–24 hours, sometimes even after 2 weeks, through poisoning by the toxins of the anaerobic soil-dwelling bacterium (Clostridium botulinuni) present in the mushroom dish.

Signs of poisoning: the person who has eaten feels nauseous, vomits, sees double, has a headache, and other signs appear similar to those caused by very poisonous mushrooms. Botulism bacteria cannot tolerate acidic (pH 4.3), salty (10 percent salt concentration) and low (4–6 °C) temperature conditions; under such conditions they do not multiply in an anaerobic environment. These bacteria live in humus-rich soil, so when using mushrooms you must in all cases clean them thoroughly and cook them well; • mushrooms gathered by children must be looked through and checked so that no inedible or even poisonous one gets in; • the stems of most mushrooms are woody and are not used for food, except that when dried they are suitable for feeding birds or livestock.

A strange and unattractive growth, dark bluish-brown, almost black, cracked and fissured, 40–50 cm in diameter, irregular in shape and not at all like a mushroom, sometimes weighing as much as 5 kg or more. It grows on living birches, more rarely on alders, rowans or other trees. Without an axe or a woodcutter's knife you cannot break it off or pull it off, only crumble its surface. Only in very rare cases does one manage to break off a larger or smaller part of it, a fragment. This fungus was noticed and described by mycologists almost 200 years ago.

More growths of various origins grow on trees, and this fungus is often confused with them. Most people know it: it is the black birch mushroom, the clinker polypore (Inonotus obliquus (Pers.) Pilat), also called "Chaga".

It is believed to cure all diseases. The spreading, woody, lumpy fungus is perennial, and its appearance is considerably influenced by sun, rain and wind. Nature gave "chagas" healing properties, thereby setting them apart from other polypores. This intricate part of the fungus consists of uneven, cross-striped layers and, most importantly, does not form or produce spores. It is a sterile form of the clinker polypore. In Lithuania only a few sites of the non-sterile form of the clinker polypore are known, but "chaga" (the sterile form) is quite common and can be found in many birch groves. So when going into the forest to look for the miraculous "chaga", you may make a mistake and cut off some other bracket fungus – these are often on the stalls at the market. On the other hand, it is possible to find genuine "chaga" at the market, but it may be old and worthless. "Chaga" is not such a miraculous fungus, although it is more valuable than other bracket fungi.

The first to take an interest in the biochemical and medicinal properties of this fungus was Prof. Dragendorff of the University of Tartu as early as 1864. He found nothing special and did not study the fungus further. There were no more thorough studies in other countries either. Only 100 years later, in 1964, did the medical institute of St Petersburg (then Leningrad) resume research on this fungus and take an interest in its medicinal properties. The institute established that this bracket fungus is extraordinary: it contains many biologically active substances – as much as 19 percent potassium and sodium, 2.45 percent magnesium oxide, 1.88 percent calcium oxide, and many pigments containing phenolic, oxyphenol-aldehyde, organic acid and other substances.

Apparently these substances are properly balanced and calm the central nervous system, improve metabolism and strengthen the immune system. Many began to regard this fungus as miraculous, but neither science nor practice has yet confirmed any extraordinary powers. Despite all the doubts, preparations such as befungin and bin-chaga have appeared. The ground fungus is recommended for treating certain diseases of the digestive tract, but when the disease is advanced, especially an oncological one, "chaga" is powerless, although for some patients it brings relief and even prolongs life. The black birch mushroom is used not only in medicine: attempts have been made to use it to improve fodder so that it stimulates the growth of livestock, especially piglets.

Only the fungus growing on birches is used for medicines and fodder. "Chagas" growing on alders, rowans, hornbeams and at the bases of old birches are not used. These fungi can be gathered all year round, but they are most valuable in winter and spring. At that time they contain the most biologically active substances. One can look for "chagas" in the forest even on the coldest winter day. For drying, the fungus is cut into 4x5 cm pieces. It cannot tolerate temperatures above 60 °C, so it is dried at a temperature no higher than 50 °C. Its active substances are retained for only 3–4 months, so it is not advisable to buy these fungi at the market, since it is unknown when they were gathered, at what temperature they were dried and on which trees they grew, and sometimes something other than this fungus is sold altogether. Dried and crushed "chaga" is kept in airtight containers in a dry place, protected from moisture and mould.

An infusion of this fungus, which contains a large amount of active substances, is used to treat chronic gastritis, gastric and duodenal ulcers and haemorrhoids; the infusion activates liver enzyme activity. Before using "chaga", even prophylactically as a tea, it is essential to consult a doctor.

Recently, ways are being sought to propagate this fungus artificially, since its natural resources in nature are small. In addition, sanitary felling in birch forests further reduces the stocks of "chaga", while the search for it is increasing.

More than 100 years ago the strong antibiotic properties of some mould fungi were noticed, and later, about 30 years afterwards, powerful antibiotics were produced – penicillin, biomycin, aureomycin and some other medicines.

The medicinal properties of macromycetes were noticed much earlier. As early as the 16th century, cep extract or powder was used to treat frostbitten, numbed parts of the body, especially the toes and fingers. A distillate of dried ceps was recommended for treating paralysed areas, as well as disorders of the circulatory organs and gastritis. It is suspected that the cep has anti-cancer properties in diseases of the stomach; for example, in Bavaria (Germany), where many ceps are eaten, stomach cancer is a rare disease.

From some funnels (Clitocybe) and knights (Tricholoma), the antibacterial substance clitocybin (elitocybiri) and others have been isolated, which inhibit the vital activity of the bacteria of skin and bone tuberculosis. Staphylococci, which cause suppurating wounds, are destroyed by extracts of the chanterelle, the yellow knight, the rufous milkcap and the wrinkled tooth fungus (raukšlėtasis dyglutis).

The common honey fungus is a laxative mushroom. An alcoholic tincture of the black witch's cauldron (Sarcosoma globosuni) was used in folk medicine for rheumatism, and its slime for treating wounds. Anti-alcohol properties are possessed not only by the common inkcap, in which the medicinal substance coprine, close to disulfiram, has been found, but also by the oak cep, the club-footed funnel, the fragrant stirnabudė (kvapioji stirnabudė) and some other mushrooms.

Muscaridine, muscarine and other substances of Amanitas are used to activate the endocrine glands and to treat sclerosis, vascular spasms and nervous diseases. Eating the lily knight (lelijinis baltikas) and the shaggy inkcap lowers blood sugar, and the true milk mushroom (piengrybis grūzdas) helps to overcome kidney stones.
Radiculitis and muscle inflammation are eased by rubbing with an alcoholic tincture of the common stinkhorn (young fruiting bodies the size and shape of a hen's egg).

According to the latest literature data, the polysaccharide lentinan, obtained from shiitake (Lentinus edodes), which is cultivated artificially in large quantities in Japan and some other places, vigorously fights lung cancer. It is claimed that some patients have even recovered. This substance also increases a patient's resistance to the AIDS virus. This mushroom ought to be grown in Lithuania as well.

Turkey tail also has anti-cancer properties. The lacquered bracket (Ganoderma lucidum) is also heavily advertised; it is recommended for weight loss, longevity and strengthening the immune system, and it is even sold in the form of powder, capsules and extracts. The last three fungi (shiitake, turkey tail and the lacquered bracket) are not only advertised but also used as capsules, powder and extract in Japan, China and other East Asian countries. For these purposes they are also cultivated artificially.
It is pleasing that scientific research into the medicinal properties of mushrooms has attracted interest in Lithuania too.

h: The Mischief of the Dry Rot Fungus

blocks.x: The dry rot fungus (Serpula lacrymans (Wulf.: Fr.) Bond.) is one of the fiercest destroyers of wood.
There are over 70 more species similar to it, mostly living in forests, parks and gardens.
However, the dry rot fungus outwits its relatives and settles in more comfortably – in houses, like some benefactor or friend.

Although it does very well in forests, where there is a lot of wood, there are also quite a few competitors there, and moreover it is quickly noticed and destroyed. Under the floors, in hidden corners and under furniture, provided the rooms are unventilated and damp, this fungus feels as if it were in paradise. Not to mention storerooms, cellars, the space under barns and unventilated attics. There it is even safer, because people cast an eye into out-of-the-way corners less often, and sometimes, by cluttering corners or covering ventilation openings, they seem to create comfortable conditions for it on purpose.

Then this fungus, which scientists also call the "weeper", quickly and firmly establishes itself under suitable conditions (30–35 percent moisture, 20–25 °C warmth). Light is not essential for it, not even necessary. The "weepers" even avoid light, because it hinders their development. By way of "thanks" for the shelter, within a few months or years this fungus turns a shed, a storeroom, floors or a corner of a house, and sometimes the whole house, into rotten debris.

It would be futile to try to compile a catalogue of tree species resistant to the dry rot fungus. There are none. Its favourites are resinous conifers, but it successfully gnaws through paper and leather, and even plaster does not stop it.

It is not difficult for this fungus to destroy a masonry wall either, as long as there is damp wood in it. Finding a crack in the wall, a larger or smaller gap and at least a piece of wood, it moves without any trouble to the second or even the third floor, and if conditions are good it climbs even higher, into the attics, where there are usually plenty of wooden structures.

The colourless hyphae of the mycelium spread both vertically and horizontally wherever it is damp, warm and unventilated. Wood turns to dust and plaster crumbles, and it makes no difference at all whether it is winter or summer.
The dry rot fungus does not damage dry, impregnated wood; it dislikes and avoids ventilated rooms. Good ventilation is fatal to the vital activity of this fungus.

The second obstacle is impregnation. There are currently enough products for impregnating wood, only one should not overdo it, because there are cases when not only dry rot fungi but also the owners cannot live in the house. The misdeeds of this fungus are described even in the Bible, where it is called "leprosy of the house". The ancient Greeks and Romans knew how to make impregnating oils whose durability has been proven by time – wooden figurines made almost 500 years before our era, which have even been in a damp environment, survive to this day.

What does this fungus look like? Its fruiting bodies resemble a sponge, 40–50 cm in diameter and 4 cm thick, irregular, most often attached to the underside of the floor, but they also occur along the walls and under the ceiling.

At first the fungus is white, later it turns brown and wrinkles radially into net-like folds, and its surface looks as if it were tearful (with droplets of brown liquid). Because of its villainy, the fungus's "tears" are called "crocodile tears". When the droplets dry and the fungus itself breathes, substances poisonous to humans are released.

So the "weepers" not only destroy the dwelling, but also harm the health of the people living in it. When the "crocodile tears" evaporate, the fungus's spores begin to fall, and they harm the eyes and the respiratory tract. In a single day just 1 cm2 of its fruiting body sheds over 35 million spores. Just imagine how many of them there are in a room. The dry rot fungus also reproduces perfectly well by fragments of vegetative mycelium on the surface of still undamaged wood. The fungus is spread by rats, mice, beetles, cats, and even by people themselves, without sensing or knowing it.

If a sickly, unpleasant smell of mould is felt in a room, or if white or brownish clusters of mycelium are visible somewhere along a wall, this dangerous focus must be destroyed as quickly as possible.

All the damaged wood must be scrupulously replaced, even though the fungus is easily cleaned off or falls off. Good ventilation is essential. Infected wood must be burned. It must not be put with firewood or with building materials, or used for household purposes.

After the plaster has been removed, the wall must be disinfected and plastered anew. Homeowners must take particular care that it is not damp under the floors and that the walls and roof space are dry.

Cellar rooms must be looked after carefully, because it is most often from there that this "benefactor" moves into living quarters. Those who have built small saunas in their homes need to be especially careful.

Mushrooms are unable to get rid of a fly that has landed on them, a mosquito, an arachnid that has crawled onto them, a millipede, a pseudoscorpion or a slug that has stuck to them, let alone springtails and other tiny beetles, and so since the very beginning of their existence they have all been forced to live together.

This is attested by the distant past – fossils from the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods, in which paleomycologists discern the imprints of dipterans and other insects feeding on fungi, especially macromycetes. Today this phenomenon is not only obvious but also well explained. Protozoa, insects, other small animals and even some of the fungi's own kin (fungi) that feed on fungi or have found shelter in them, some even spending their whole life there, are called mycetobionts.

The way of life of fungi, especially the speed of formation and growth and the lifespan of the fruiting body, depends heavily on environmental conditions (the amount of warmth and moisture), and therefore some mycetobionts have also had to change their way of life and adapt by shortening their life cycle. First of all, those that are directly linked to the biological age of the fungal fruiting body. Incidentally, the mycetobionts, some more, some less, repay the fungi by dispersing their spores. For example, 200 species of dipteran insects alone maintain close ties with cap mushrooms – some feeding on them, others hiding from enemies in them, and still others spending one or another stage of development, or even their whole life, in the fruiting body.

The biological and physiological features of mycetobionts and their way of life have been studied reasonably well. Some insects can have several generations during the fungal growing season, others 2–3, and still others only one.

Some choose only the caps and lay their eggs only in them, from which voracious larvae develop; others choose only the stems; others both caps and stems; and there are also those that choose only the vegetative mycelium at the base of the stem (in the substrate).

One would think that the cep is attacked by 60 insect species, the slippery jack by 32, all the boletes by over 100, and the gilled mushrooms by 133 species of dipteran insects alone. Brittlegills alone are attacked by more than 30 species. Field mushrooms have far fewer "offenders" or "cohabitants" than brittlegills. Morels and false morels also have quite a few "offenders" or "tenants" – more than 50 species. Puffballs, bovists and other gasteromycetes, on the other hand, are disliked by insects; only the odd species visits them, feasting on their soft, rich trama without lingering long. The chanterelle is also disliked: only 3–4 species of "offenders" taste its trama, and even then, as if "afraid", they mostly bore only into the stem.

It has been established that some mycetobionts are content with some fungi, others with other fungi, while still others – the least choosy – do not distinguish between fungal species. For example, Mycetophila jungorum is aggressively disposed and attacks as many as 100 species of agaricoid fungi.

There are also those that have chosen only 1–2 fungal species. Lower mycetobiont activity has been observed at the beginning and end of the fungal growing season. There seems to be an inverse relationship between the mushroom crop and the activity and intensity of the mycetobionts. The larger the mushroom crop, the less they are attacked (get maggoty), although this is not confirmed every year.

It is supposed that fungi release certain attractant substances that help female mycetobionts find their way in the depths of the forest, and even lure them to find a suitable mushroom in which to lay their eggs, while at the same time carrying away that mushroom's spores and extending its range. It is an interesting phenomenon, it is being studied, and it has good prospects for the future in protecting ceps and other valuable mushrooms from an excessive horde of "offenders", which sometimes destroy as much as about 60–70 percent of the crop not only of ceps but of other mushrooms too. However, this is responsible and rather complex work, requiring prior clarification of the biology of the harmful insects, their biotope attachment, seasonal activity, their relationships with other mycetobionts, and their significance in the life of the forest and in the biogeocoenosis. Sometimes, by breaking one vital link in a biocoenosis, one can bring about even more undesirable phenomena.

Among the mycetobionts there are also good-for-nothings from among the fungi's own kin – mostly ascomycetes of the genus Hypomyces. When warm and humid weather persists, favourable conditions arise for these fungi to carry out their wicked designs. You will often come across a leaning birch bolete, deformed green, red-stemmed or brown-capped Xerocomus boletes, the grey rollrim, some brittlegills, not infrequently a cep, a slippery jack or even a chanterelle, and other mushrooms.

The favourite underside of the cap (gills, tubes) becomes covered with a film of white, yellow or pinkish parasitic mould, and not infrequently the attacked mushroom looks as if it had turned horny. Affected mushrooms are unfit for food and are sometimes even poisonous. The most widespread ascomycete is Apiocrea chrysosperma (Tul.) Syd., and in its conidial stage Sepedonium chrysospermum (Bull.) Fr. Although this lurker does the most damage to mushrooms, it looks gentler than the parasitic bolete (Xerocmusparasiticus (Bull.: Fr.) Quel.), which parasitises the common earthball (Scleroderma au-rantium Pers). Who would think that a mushroom of bolete origin, and an edible one at that, destroys a poisonous gasteromycete by settling on its root base. It is very rare, found only once (Anykščiai district). Or the powdery piggyback (Asterophora lycoperdoides (Bull.) Ditm.), but this one, as a saprotroph, has linked its life mostly only with dead brittlegills, especially the blackening brittlegill and the fading brittlegill. I once observed how the piggyback had "occupied" more than 60 fruiting bodies of the fading brittlegill in one entire compartment of bilberry pine forest in the Daunoriai forest district of Aukštaitija National Park. There are also more cannibal fungi that are fond of their living and dead kin.

Incidentally, roe deer, elk, wild boar, squirrels, voles, jays, thrushes and some other forest dwellers sometimes feast on mushrooms out of curiosity, sometimes to satisfy their hunger, and sometimes when they are unwell. Squirrels eat the most mushrooms.

Research on mycetobionts has been carried out only quite recently; it began only in the 1970s (in Germany, Finland, Hungary, England and Russia). It is gratifying that in recent years it has also been carried out in Lithuania (Institute of Ecology).
